title: Interview opening and the rainy Baton Rouge Masonic parade
summary: Allen opens the tape (808 Royal Street, 13 July 1961) and asks about a rained-out parade in Baton Rouge; Robinson explains wet drumheads can burst.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: This is a real one Jim Robinson and we're at 808 Royal Street. Today is July what is it? 13th. Yeah July the 13th 1961. My name is Dick Allen so put your name on that too. Jim Robinson. Say it again? Jim Robinson. Okay. Okay now we'll sit back and relax. A lot of things to talk about. We're talking about Baton Rouge. You got up there a couple of years ago on a parade. What happened?

Oh that, you had to wash out. The Masonic parade. Four bands. That was a large parade. A bad day for it. The rain but that didn't stop the parade. People made the parade the day. After we all, sun come out and we got dry and came, got the bus and came on back home. What bands was that? It was the Tuxedo and the Ricker. It was a school band. Two school bands. I don't know the name of the school bands.
I see. So anyway, how do you like playing when the drums get wet? What does that do?

Well, you don't get no effect. You see, because the fella can't hit the drum too loud because they must bust the drum. You know, the head is wet and they'll bust the head. So I figure this way, when a parade like that, drums is the main thing in the parade, you know. When the drums go to drum is, you can't play the music like you want to play because the drums just keep the time. So when the head gets wet like that's the day you think, you might bust it at any minute.
